Weighted Data Selection:
Sharp Upper-Half and Five-Dimensional Laws

Zhongxuan Liu    Hongzhi Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Faculty of Computing, Harbin Institute of Technology Email: lazrix@163.com    wangzh@hit.edu.cn
Abstract

How much risk does a small reweighted training support retain? For finite weighted least squares with the minimum-norm learner, we prove the exact law Γd​(n)=3−n/d\Gamma_{d}(n)=3-n/d throughout ⌈3​d/2⌉≤n≤2​d−1\lceil 3d/2\rceil\leq n\leq 2d-1. The guarantee covers every observed feature rank and uses selections that preserve the full feature span. Balanced simplex anchors reduce dimension; positive-weight lifting and independent-line compression close the risk bound. Shifted coordinate pairs attain the matching lower bound. The complete dataset-level upper bound and sharpness construction are verified in Lean 4. At the smaller budget (d,n)=(5,6)(d,n)=(5,6), we also prove Γ5​(6)=11/5\Gamma_{5}(6)=11/5, matching the simplex-block prediction from 5=3+25=3+2 over arbitrary interacting configurations. Circuit covers, comparison second moments, and circuit-plane probabilities give the sharp excess 6/56/5, while polar-face geometry resolves shared rank-three circuits. The general simplex-block frontier connects these laws within the intermediate-budget selection problem.

1 Introduction

Data selection changes the training data while keeping the learner fixed. For least squares, a selector can retain a few original examples and assign them new positive weights. The question is how well the resulting predictor performs on the full dataset. This separates the information carried by a small training support from the computational method used to find it. In the very small-support regime, even the rule for choosing among multiple least-squares solutions matters: balancing the selected gradients need not recover the full solution if the selected feature span loses rank.

We study exact worst-case risk inflation for the minimum-norm learner. The evaluation weights pp specify the target finite distribution; they may encode multiplicities or importance weights. The training weights qq are the selector’s decision variables. This distinction lets a small support represent a nonuniform target without changing the evaluation criterion. The guarantee concerns this finite-distribution risk, rather than population generalization or the running time of a selection algorithm.

We establish two sharp laws for arbitrary weighted configurations. Throughout the upper half of the intermediate-budget interval, Γd​(n)=3−n/d\Gamma_{d}(n)=3-n/d for ⌈3​d/2⌉≤n≤2​d−1\lceil 3d/2\rceil\leq n\leq 2d-1. Balanced anchors and full-span lifting give a dimension induction whose complete dataset-level statement is verified in Lean 4. At the smaller budget (d,n)=(5,6)(d,n)=(5,6), the unrestricted bound Γ5​(6)≤11/5\Gamma_{5}(6)\leq 11/5 matches a seven-point example. This second result handles intersecting positive circuits through more detailed five-dimensional geometry.

Prior results and the precise addition.

Hanneke et al. (2025a) established the uniform-evaluation endpoints Γd​(d)=d+1\Gamma_{d}(d)=d+1 and exact recovery at 2​d2d; the companion open problem asked about intermediate budgets (Hanneke et al., 2025b). Table 1 separates the results used here from the five-dimensional upper bound. In particular, the value 11/511/5 as a lower bound is already present in Zhang (2026), version 1, via its simplex-block construction. That work also proves the boundary law and the four-dimensional five-point law. We use its latter theorem as an input. Our contribution at (5,6)(5,6) is the universal matching upper bound, together with a self-contained weighted, minimum-norm-safe matching example.

A training-realization viewpoint.

The proof asks which low-risk geometric points can actually be returned by the stipulated learner. A positive circuit of rank rr has r+1r+1 rows whose positive weighted sum is zero. Combining it with 5−r5-r independent interpolating rows gives a six-row full-rank training problem. This interface allows polar geometry, comparison second moments, and circuit-plane graphs to control the risk of actual fits. The main text derives both sources of the sharp excess 6/56/5 and states the exhaustive classification connecting them. The appendix retains the full shared-circuit analysis rather than assuming that all instances split into independent blocks.

The same concern with realizability motivates our complementary certificate theory. Full-span certificate complexity identifies when exact recovery is available and when maximal complexity forces independent one-dimensional blocks. Exact one-point penalties on those blocks yield the weighted boundary law and its extremal conditions. Thus the boundary and interior results share an interface between positive dependence and the output of a fixed learner, while requiring different geometry.

Relation to approximation and sampling.

Regression coresets approximate a full objective or its solution (Feldman & Langberg, 2011; Drineas et al., 2006; Dasgupta et al., 2009; Boutsidis et al., 2013). Sketching and leverage-based methods provide computational and statistical guarantees (Clarkson & Woodruff, 2009; Clarkson & Woodruff, 2017; Pilanci & Wainwright, 2015; Ma et al., 2015; Raskutti & Mahoney, 2016); volume sampling gives randomized subset guarantees (Dereziński & Warmuth, 2018). Here we instead determine a deterministic infimum over reweighted original supports at a fixed small budget, including deficient-rank designs. Positive-basis theory (Davis, 1954; Nævdal, 2019) supplies geometric inputs; the additional requirement is to implement the resulting certificate by positive-weight training with the correct minimum-norm output.

2 Problem and sharp intermediate-budget laws

Let D={(xi,yi,pi)}i=1ND=\{(x_{i},y_{i},p_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, with xi∈ℝdx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, yi∈ℝy_{i}\in\mathbb{R}, pi>0p_{i}>0, and ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1. Write [N]={1,…,N}[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\} and define

LD​(w)=∑ipi​(xi⊤​w−yi)2,w⋆=arg​minminimum norm,w⁡LD​(w),LD⋆=LD​(w⋆).L_{D}(w)=\sum_{i}p_{i}(x_{i}^{\top}w-y_{i})^{2},\qquad w^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\text{minimum norm},\,w}L_{D}(w),\qquad L_{D}^{\star}=L_{D}(w^{\star}).

Minimum norm is the generalized-inverse least-squares convention (Penrose, 1955; Penrose, 1956). Set U=span⁡{xi}U=\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}\}; then w⋆∈Uw^{\star}\in U. For q∈ΔN={q≥0:∑iqi=1}q\in\Delta_{N}=\{q\geq 0:\sum_{i}q_{i}=1\}, let w^​(q)\widehat{w}(q) be the minimum-norm minimizer of ∑iqi​(xi⊤​w−yi)2\sum_{i}q_{i}(x_{i}^{\top}w-y_{i})^{2}. Only positive support entries count toward the budget. Define

LD⋆​(n,A⋆)=infq∈ΔN|supp⁡(q)|≤nLD​(w^​(q)),L_{D}^{\star}(n;A^{\star})=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\in\Delta_{N}\\ |\operatorname{supp}(q)|\leq n\end{subarray}}L_{D}(\widehat{w}(q)), (1)
Γd(n)=supD:LD⋆>0LD⋆​(n,A⋆)LD⋆.\Gamma_{d}(n)=\sup_{D:L_{D}^{\star}>0}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n;A^{\star})}{L_{D}^{\star}}. (2)

The evaluation weights stay equal to pp, even though training uses qq. We keep an infimum because minimum-norm solutions can jump at a rank change. When LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}=0, selecting a basis of UU with arbitrary positive weights recovers w⋆w^{\star}: the selected solutions are w⋆+U⟂w^{\star}+U^{\perp}, whose minimum-norm point is w⋆w^{\star}. Thus zero optimal risk is recovered at budgets n≥dn\geq d; the zero-rank case is immediate.

Theorem 1 (Upper-half intermediate-budget law).

For d≥2d\geq 2 and 1≤t≤⌊d/2⌋1\leq t\leq\lfloor d/2\rfloor,

Γd​(2​d−t)=1+td,equivalentlyΓd​(n)=3−nd(⌈3​d/2⌉≤n≤2​d−1).\Gamma_{d}(2d-t)=1+\frac{t}{d},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\Gamma_{d}(n)=3-\frac{n}{d}\quad(\lceil 3d/2\rceil\leq n\leq 2d-1).

For every finite weighted instance with LD⋆>0L_{D}^{\star}>0 and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is q∈ΔNq\in\Delta_{N} with |supp⁡(q)|≤2​d−t|\operatorname{supp}(q)|\leq 2d-t and Uq=UU_{q}=U such that LD​(w^​(q))≤(1+t/d+ε)​LD⋆L_{D}(\widehat{w}(q))\leq(1+t/d+\varepsilon)L_{D}^{\star}. Uniform pairs (ej,1),(ej,3)(e_{j},1),(e_{j},3) attain the matching lower bound.

Appendix C proves the theorem by dimension induction. A balanced aa-dimensional simplex fixes an anchor, and a full-rank selection in its orthogonal complement lifts to the original problem. The budget and risk ratios close when d≥2​td\geq 2t. Maximal certificates reduce to independent lines, where compressing the tt least costly lines gives excess at most (t/d)​LD⋆(t/d)L_{D}^{\star}. The Lean 4 proof includes zero residuals, deficient ranks, normalized weights, and the stipulated minimum-norm rule.

Theorem 2 (Five-dimensional six-point law).

For the weighted minimum-norm selection problem in Equation 2,

Γ5​(6)=115.\Gamma_{5}(6)=\frac{11}{5}.

More precisely, for every finite instance in ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5} and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, a selection of at most six points, with strictly positive weights on its support, satisfies LD​(w^)≤(11/5+ε)​LD⋆L_{D}(\widehat{w})\leq(11/5+\varepsilon)L_{D}^{\star}. For positive observed feature rank, the selection can span that feature space. A seven-point instance attains the ratio 11/511/5.

The upper bound makes no separation assumption on the features. Full span is essential to the proof: every approximating training objective has a unique minimizer on UU, so it returns the required minimum-norm vector. The statement allows a limiting sequence; it does not assert that every instance attains its selected infimum. By contrast, the lower-bound example below attains the exact ratio with a finite selection.

2.1 Intermediate-budget landscape

Write n=d+sn=d+s, where 0≤s≤d−10\leq s\leq d-1. A block of dimension aa can be represented exactly by its a+1a+1 circuit rows. Spending only aa rows incurs excess at most aa times its optimal block loss. The budget d+sd+s therefore allows ss blocks to receive the extra row. This allocation problem leads to

Φd,s=maxs<k≤da1+⋯+ak=daj∈ℕ>0⁡k−s∑j=1kaj−1.\Phi_{d,s}=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}s<k\leq d\\ a_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}=d\\ a_{j}\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\end{subarray}}\frac{k-s}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{j}^{-1}}. (3)

Let Γd⊕​(n)\Gamma_{d}^{\oplus}(n) restrict (2) to orthogonal sums of simplex circuits: block jj consists of aj+1a_{j}+1 feature rows, spans an aja_{j}-dimensional subspace, and every aja_{j} rows form a basis; its nonzero residual-gradient atoms form a positive circuit at the block optimum. Evaluation weights and labels may vary within this class.

Proposition 3 (General lower bound and exact block frontier).

For d≥1d\geq 1 and 0≤s≤d−10\leq s\leq d-1,

Γd​(d+s)≥1+Φd,s,Γd⊕​(d+s)=1+Φd,s.\Gamma_{d}(d+s)\geq 1+\Phi_{d,s},\qquad\Gamma_{d}^{\oplus}(d+s)=1+\Phi_{d,s}. (4)

Appendix D gives the block allocation proof and a translated construction that also excludes deficient-rank selections. These recover the block lower bound and structured frontier of Zhang (2026, Proposition 12, Theorem 15, Corollary 16) in the present weighted model. Their role here is to identify the extremal prediction tested by the new unrestricted upper bound.

For s=1s=1, Φd,1=⌊d2/4⌋/d\Phi_{d,1}=\lfloor d^{2}/4\rfloor/d for d≥2d\geq 2. In particular, at d=5d=5 the partition 3+23+2 gives

c=(1/3+1/2)−1=6/5,(ℓ3,ℓ2)=(c/3,c/2)=(2/5,3/5).c=(1/3+1/2)^{-1}=6/5,\qquad(\ell_{3},\ell_{2})=(c/3,c/2)=(2/5,3/5). (5)

The extra row completes one block, while the other contributes 6/56/5. Theorem 2 proves that arbitrary interacting circuits obey the same worst-case value. The three-plus-two upper-bound cover below recovers precisely this balancing mechanism.

The frontier also gives Φd,0=d\Phi_{d,0}=d and Φd,d−1=1/d\Phi_{d,d-1}=1/d. These match the endpoint and the penultimate boundary, respectively; full-span certificates give exact recovery at n≥2​dn\geq 2d. Theorem 1 settles the whole upper-half interval; Theorem 2 settles (5,6)(5,6) below it. The general equality Γd​(d+s)=1+Φd,s\Gamma_{d}(d+s)=1+\Phi_{d,s} remains the target for the other intermediate budgets. Appendix D.5 gives its matrix formulation.

2.2 Proof architecture

Figure 2 organizes the two sharp laws into separate proof routes. The upper route combines full-span certificates, balanced anchors, and independent-line compression through dimension induction. The lower route classifies normalized five-dimensional systems and transfers realizable fits back to regression. Each universal upper bound is paired with its matching lower-bound construction.

A positive circuit is a support-minimal positive zero relation among roots. A circuit AA of rank rr has r+1r+1 roots. Every root belongs to a circuit, since the strictly positive zero relation in (6) decomposes into extreme rays of its nonnegative relation cone.

Lemma 4 (From a circuit to an actual fit).

Let AA be a rank-rr positive circuit with span PP, and let JJ be 5−r5-r roots independent modulo PP. If vj⊤​z=1v_{j}^{\top}z=1 for j∈Jj\in J and vi⊤​z≤1v_{i}^{\top}z\leq 1 for i∈Ai\in A, then zz is a limit of positive-weight full-rank training outputs on A∪JA\cup J.

Proof.

Take ci>0c_{i}>0 with ∑i∈Aci​vi=0\sum_{i\in A}c_{i}v_{i}=0, and let z0∈P⟂z_{0}\in P^{\perp} interpolate JJ. Then zϵ=(1−ϵ)​z+ϵ​z0z_{\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon)z+\epsilon z_{0} still interpolates JJ and has vi⊤​zϵ<1v_{i}^{\top}z_{\epsilon}<1 on AA. Set

wi=ci1−vi⊤​zϵ(i∈A)w_{i}=\frac{c_{i}}{1-v_{i}^{\top}z_{\epsilon}}\quad(i\in A)

and give the interpolated rows arbitrary positive weights. The gradient is −2∑i∈Acivi=0-2\sum_{i\in A}c_{i}v_{i}=0. Since the selected rows span ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}, this stationary point is the unique minimizer. The support size is (r+1)+(5−r)=6(r+1)+(5-r)=6. Let ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0. ∎

This argument is dimension-independent with 55 replaced by dd and support budget d+1d+1. The remaining challenge is to find a low-norm point meeting its interpolation and one-sided circuit inequalities.

3 The exhaustive geometry behind the upper bound

Call a root good if it is a strictly positive combination of five other independent roots; call the remaining roots exceptional, and denote their set by EE. Put K=conv⁡{±vi}K=\operatorname{conv}\{\pm v_{i}\}. A good root on ∂K\partial K yields δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1 by a supporting functional and an explicit six-row fit. Otherwise the exceptional roots generate KK and admit a comparison second moment

K=conv⁡{±e:e∈E},C=∑e∈Eμe​e​e⊤⪰I5,μe≥0,∑eμe=1.K=\operatorname{conv}\{\pm e:e\in E\},\qquad C=\sum_{e\in E}\mu_{e}ee^{\top}\succeq I_{5},\qquad\mu_{e}\geq 0,\quad\sum_{e}\mu_{e}=1. (7)

Indeed, express each original root as a convex combination of signed exceptional roots and average the quadratic Jensen inequalities with λi\lambda_{i}. The measure μ\mu need not have mean zero. This distinction is important when it is used for interpolation below; it is a second moment comparison, not a centered-covariance replacement. Appendix B.1 supplies the boundary-root construction.

Proposition 5 (Exhaustive circuit-rank split).

For every finite root system satisfying (6), exactly one of the following circuit configurations occurs.

  1. (i)

    A positive circuit has rank four or five. Then δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1.

  2. (ii)

    All circuits have rank at most three, and two rank-three circuits share a root and jointly span ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}. Then δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1.

  3. (iii)

    A rank-three circuit exists, every circuit has rank at most three, and the shared-root configuration in (ii) is absent. Then either the two-line quotient argument gives δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1, or two circuit spans of dimensions three and two cover EE, giving δ6≤6/5\delta_{6}\leq 6/5.

  4. (iv)

    All circuits have rank at most two. Either a four-plus-one decomposition (or an independent-line system) gives δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1, or the circuit-plane graph gives δ6≤6/5\delta_{6}\leq 6/5.

In (ii)–(iii), the good-boundary-root alternative is first discharged with bound one; the exceptional-root assertions concern the other alternative.

Why the split is sufficient.

The four configurations are disjoint and exhaustive by the maximum circuit rank and the presence of a shared-root rank-three pair. A rank-five circuit trains exactly at zero. For a rank-four circuit, one maximum absolute normal projection supplies the interpolating row and squared norm at most one. The shared-root case is handled by signed polar faces, as explained below and proved in Appendix B.3. For (iii), quotienting by a rank-three circuit either yields only two independent lines, or yields a seven-root positive generating subset. The two extreme rays of its relation cone have supports of sizes (4,3)(4,3), disjoint, or (4,4)(4,4), sharing one root. The latter is excluded by (iii). In the former, any crossing exceptional root either forces the forbidden shared-root pair or reduces all exceptional projections to two quotient lines; with no crossing exceptional roots the (3,2)(3,2) cover remains. The support and crossing arguments are given in Appendix B.5. Finally, circuit-plane intersections give the alternatives in (iv), proved in Appendix B.4. The next two subsections derive the constant in the branches that need the full excess 6/56/5.

3.1 First mechanism: a three-plus-two cover

For any rank-rr anchor circuit with span PP, the comparison measure gives

δ6≤(5−r)​μ​(E∖P).\delta_{6}\leq(5-r)\mu(E\setminus P). (8)

To see why this remains valid for a noncentered measure, project its roots onto P⟂P^{\perp} and write their second moment as B=∑iηi​zi​zi⊤≻0B=\sum_{i}\eta_{i}z_{i}z_{i}^{\top}\succ 0, total mass as a=∑iηia=\sum_{i}\eta_{i}, and first moment as b=∑iηi​zib=\sum_{i}\eta_{i}z_{i}. Determinant-weighted sampling of k=5−rk=5-r independent rows yields interpolants tJt_{J} satisfying

𝔼⁡[tJ⊤​B​tJ]≤k​a−(k−1)​b⊤​B−1​b≤k​a.\mathbb{E}[t_{J}^{\top}Bt_{J}]\leq ka-(k-1)b^{\top}B^{-1}b\leq ka. (9)

This follows by comparing the coefficient of a common rank-one row translation in the Cauchy–Binet identity; singular subsets contribute nonnegative terms (Lemma 16). Since BB dominates the identity on P⟂P^{\perp}, some interpolant has squared norm at most k​aka. Its anchor evaluations are zero, so Lemma 4 gives an actual admissible fit. Only roots outside PP enter aa, proving (8).

Now let circuit spans PA,PBP_{A},P_{B} of dimensions three and two cover EE. Write α=μ⁡(E∖PA)\alpha=\mu(E\setminus P_{A}) and β=μ⁡(E∖PB)\beta=\mu(E\setminus P_{B}). The two outside sets are disjoint, so α+β≤1\alpha+\beta\leq 1. Apply (8) to each anchor:

δ6≤min⁡{2​α,3​β}≤min⁡{2​α,3​(1−α)}≤65.\delta_{6}\leq\min\{2\alpha,3\beta\}\leq\min\{2\alpha,3(1-\alpha)\}\leq\frac{6}{5}. (10)

The last maximum occurs when 2​α=3​(1−α)2\alpha=3(1-\alpha), that is, α=3/5\alpha=3/5. This explains the constant without assuming the comparison measure is centered or replacing the original risk by a block surrogate. The same calculation for a (3,3)(3,3) cover gives bound one.

3.2 Second mechanism: circuit-plane graphs and actual risk

Suppose all circuits have rank at most two. Form a graph GG whose vertices are distinct planes of rank-two circuits, joining two planes when their intersection is zero. If GG has a triangle or four-cycle, the circuit geometry forces every root into a four-space and a complementary line. Their evaluation second moments are orthogonal projections, so the four-dimensional five-row input and one interpolated line use six rows with total excess at most one.

Otherwise GG has no triangles or four-cycles. Neighbors of a vertex are pairwise intersecting planes. They either share a line or lie in a three-space. Circuit elimination bounds these alternatives by two and three neighbors, respectively (Lemma 19), hence Δ⁡(G)≤3\Delta(G)\leq 3. If there are no circuit planes, all roots lie on five independent lines and the maximum-absolute-coefficient interpolant gives bound one. We therefore consider a nonempty GG.

Lemma 6 (Graph probability).

Every nonempty finite graph with no triangles or four-cycles and Δ⁡(G)≤3\Delta(G)\leq 3 admits a probability θ\theta on its vertices with

∑A∼BθA−θB≤15for every ​B.\sum_{A\sim B}\theta_{A}-\theta_{B}\leq\frac{1}{5}\quad\text{for every }B. (11)
Proof.

If a vertex has degree three, put mass 2/52/5 on it and 1/51/5 on each neighbor. Every exterior vertex meets at most one of those neighbors, since two would form a four-cycle. This proves the bound everywhere. If the maximum degree is at most two, choose one path or cycle component. Use the uniform probability on a cycle of length at least five. For paths on one through four vertices use, respectively, (1)(1), (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2), (2/7,3/7,2/7)(2/7,3/7,2/7), and (1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6). For longer paths put 1/51/5 on five consecutive vertices. All other vertices have zero mass; direct substitution proves the claim, including vertices just outside the positive-mass segment. ∎

The constant 1/51/5 is sharp for this abstract graph statement: on a five-cycle, summing its five left sides gives one for every probability, so their maximum is at least 1/51/5, and uniform mass attains it. This observation is not a claim that every eligible graph is realizable by a normalized root system, nor a separate regression lower bound.

Why this graph controls training risk.

Choose an actual triangle circuit as anchor for each graph vertex AA. The polytope

𝒫A={z∈PA⟂:vi⊤​z≤1​ for every ​i}\mathcal{P}_{A}=\{z\in P_{A}^{\perp}:v_{i}^{\top}z\leq 1\text{ for every }i\}

is bounded and three-dimensional. Express zero as a convex combination of its vertices. Each vertex interpolates three rows independent modulo PAP_{A}; together with the zero-evaluation anchor it is an actual full-rank six-row fit. This finite distribution has 𝔼A​z=0\mathbb{E}_{A}z=0.

For a circuit BB with normalized coefficients βi\beta_{i}, let ρA​B=dimPB−dim(PA∩PB)\rho_{AB}=\dim P_{B}-\dim(P_{A}\cap P_{B}). Project the positive relation of BB modulo PAP_{A} and decompose it into projected circuits. On one such circuit with coefficients αi\alpha_{i} and support size ss, write Ti=vi⊤​zT_{i}=v_{i}^{\top}z. We have Ti≤1T_{i}\leq 1, ∑iαi​Ti=0\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}T_{i}=0 pointwise, and 𝔼A​Ti=0\mathbb{E}_{A}T_{i}=0. Consequently

−1−αiαi≤Ti≤1,𝔼A​Ti2≤1−αiαi,𝔼A​∑iαi​Ti2≤s−1≤ρA​B.-\frac{1-\alpha_{i}}{\alpha_{i}}\leq T_{i}\leq 1,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{A}T_{i}^{2}\leq\frac{1-\alpha_{i}}{\alpha_{i}},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{A}\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}T_{i}^{2}\leq s-1\leq\rho_{AB}.

The second inequality follows by averaging (Ti+(1−αi)/αi)​(Ti−1)≤0(T_{i}+(1-\alpha_{i})/\alpha_{i})(T_{i}-1)\leq 0. Reassembling the projected circuits, whose total mass is at most one, gives 𝔼A​∑i∈Bβi​(vi⊤​z)2≤ρA​B\mathbb{E}_{A}\sum_{i\in B}\beta_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}z)^{2}\leq\rho_{AB}. For rank-two BB,

ρA​B=1+𝟏A∼B−𝟏PA=PB,∑AθA​ρA​B≤1+15=65;\rho_{AB}=1+\boldsymbol{1}_{A\sim B}-\boldsymbol{1}_{P_{A}=P_{B}},\qquad\sum_{A}\theta_{A}\rho_{AB}\leq 1+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{6}{5};

for rank-one BB the same average is at most one. Decompose the original zero-mean probability λ\lambda into normalized positive circuits and mix the anchor distributions according to θ\theta. The original second moment in (6) now gives

𝔼​‖z‖2=𝔼​∑iλi​(vi⊤​z)2≤65.\mathbb{E}\|z\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}z)^{2}\leq\frac{6}{5}. (12)

Some fit in this finite distribution therefore has excess at most 6/56/5. Thus the graph bound controls the risk of realizable training outputs, not merely a numerical quantity attached to circuit intersections.

3.3 The shared-root branch: the invariant that closes the cases

Two rank-three circuits sharing a root and spanning five dimensions can, for incidence calculations, be positively rescaled to

u+a0+a1+a2=0,u+b0+b1+b2=0.u+a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}=0,\qquad u+b_{0}+b_{1}+b_{2}=0.

Additional roots cannot simply be discarded. The proof classifies each crossing exceptional root into three forms, then checks which forms can coexist. A forbidden coexistence either makes a root good or creates a circuit of rank four or five. These are the invariant exclusion tests behind the algebra in Appendix B.3.

The remaining configurations give a cover by two rank-three spans, a three-span cover, a four-span configuration, or two quotient lines. For the middle two, use the symmetric polar Q={z:|e⊤​z|≤1​(e∈E)}Q=\{z:|e^{\top}z|\leq 1\ (e\in E)\}. At a vertex, color active roots by their signs. If neither sign supplies two independent interpolating roots modulo an available rank-three circuit, the active roots outside the shared two-space must all have one unoriented direction (Lemma 17). On the relevant polar slice, switching that direction would activate two nonparallel roots and violate the restriction. This forces a realizable face or vertex. Its squared norm is at most one by the original normalization.

This reasoning explains why the branch tolerates arbitrary extra rows: the active-space restriction is applied to all exceptional roots, and their signed hull contains every original root. Positive rescaling is used only for dependence signs, ranks, and spans; it is never used to claim that the original quadratic risk is unchanged. Table 2 indexes the structural proof obligations.

4 Transfer, attainment, and the matching example

The root bound covers all normalized systems by Proposition 5. To recover every regression instance, one must also handle rows for which division by ηi\eta_{i} is invalid. If η0=0\eta_{0}=0 and ξ0≠0\xi_{0}\neq 0, constrain zz to ξ0⟂\xi_{0}^{\perp} and apply the four-dimensional five-row theorem there. Lift those rows and add row zero with weight M>0M>0. The resulting full-rank objective converges, as M→∞M\to\infty, to the constrained fit and gives ratio infimum at most two. Every finite MM is an admissible six-row design. Pure-residual rows (ξi=0\xi_{i}=0, ηi≠0\eta_{i}\neq 0) only reduce the nonzero-root mass to a≤1a\leq 1; renormalizing and scaling gives excess at most 6​a/5≤6/56a/5\leq 6/5. Deficient observed ranks use the four-dimensional input, the dimension-three boundary law, or exact certificates in ranks at most two. Appendix B.6 proves these transfers, including the extension of the uniform four-dimensional input to arbitrary positive evaluation weights. Thus the root construction proves the full upper bound in Theorem 2.

For the lower bound take the seven feature rows

e1,e2,e3,−e1−e2−e3,e4,e5,−e4−e5,e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},-e_{1}-e_{2}-e_{3},\qquad e_{4},e_{5},-e_{4}-e_{5},

with evaluation weights 1/101/10 on each of the first four and 1/51/5 on each of the last three. Put h=(10,20,40,80,160)⊤h=(10,20,40,80,160)^{\top} and yi=xi⊤​h+1y_{i}=x_{i}^{\top}h+1. Then w⋆=hw^{\star}=h, LD⋆=1L_{D}^{\star}=1, and the blocks have dimensions three and two and total masses 2/52/5 and 3/53/5. Any full-rank support of size at most six leaves one block with exactly its dimension rr rows. Those rows interpolate at displacement one, forcing the omitted simplex row to have displacement −r-r. Its block excess is ar​(r+r2)/(r+1)=ar​r=6/5a_{r}(r+r^{2})/(r+1)=a_{r}r=6/5. Retaining the full tetrahedron with equal training weights and two triangle rows attains this value. The translation by hh makes every deficient selected span incur excess at least five, so minimum-norm rank loss cannot improve it. The exact distance argument is in Appendix B.7. This proves both attainment for the example and Γ5​(6)≥11/5\Gamma_{5}(6)\geq 11/5. It is the 3+23+2 optimizer in (5), with the generic translation replaced by an explicit vector.

5 Certificate rigidity and the penultimate boundary

The boundary theory gives a complementary, dimension-uniform account of realizability. Define the residual-scaled features by

ri=xi⊤​w⋆−yi,gi=ri​xi,r_{i}=x_{i}^{\top}w^{\star}-y_{i},\qquad g_{i}=r_{i}x_{i}, (13)

so the normal equations give

∑ipi​gi=0.\sum_{i}p_{i}g_{i}=0. (14)

For Uq=span⁡{xi:qi>0}U_{q}=\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:q_{i}>0\}, exact minimum-norm recovery is equivalent to

w^(q)=w⋆⟺∑iqigi=0andw⋆∈Uq.\widehat{w}(q)=w^{\star}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{i}q_{i}g_{i}=0\ \text{and}\ w^{\star}\in U_{q}.

Stationarity is the first condition; orthogonality to the selected Hessian’s kernel is the second. A full-span certificate enforces the stronger condition Uq=UU_{q}=U. Let κ⁡(D)\kappa(D) be its minimum support size. Theorems 7–10 give

m≤κ(D)≤m+r≤2m≤2d(m=dimU≥1,r=dimspan{gi:gi≠0}),m\leq\kappa(D)\leq m+r\leq 2m\leq 2d\quad(m=\dim U\geq 1,\ r=\dim\operatorname{span}\{g_{i}:g_{i}\neq 0\}),

with κ⁡(D)=1\kappa(D)=1 when m=0m=0. Steinitz compression (Steinitz, 1916; Ivanov & Naszódi, 2024) and maximal positive-basis rigidity imply that κ⁡(D)=2​m\kappa(D)=2m holds exactly when the nonzero features lie on mm independent lines and all have nonzero gradients. Both directions, including extra mixed features and zero-gradient rows, are proved in Appendix A.

On this rigid branch the risk is C0+∑j=1mLj​(tj)C_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}L_{j}(t_{j}), with Lj​(t)=∑iai​(t−zi)2L_{j}(t)=\sum_{i}a_{i}(t-z_{i})^{2}, ai>0a_{i}>0. If Aj=∑iaiA_{j}=\sum_{i}a_{i} and μj=∑iai​zi/Aj\mu_{j}=\sum_{i}a_{i}z_{i}/A_{j}, the exact one-point penalty is

δj=Aj​mini​(zi−μj)2≤Lj⋆.\delta_{j}=A_{j}\min_{i}(z_{i}-\mu_{j})^{2}\leq L_{j}^{\star}.

Two points recover μj\mu_{j} exactly. Equality in the penalty bound, for positive block loss, occurs precisely at two equidistant target levels of equal effective mass (Theorem 11). If κ⁡(D)≤2​d−1\kappa(D)\leq 2d-1, selection is exact; otherwise, compress the least costly of the dd lines to one point and retain two points on each other line. The resulting positive-weight full-span fit satisfies

LD⋆​(2​d−1,A⋆)≤LD⋆+minj⁡δj≤LD⋆+1d​∑jLj⋆≤(1+1/d)​LD⋆.L_{D}^{\star}(2d-1;A^{\star})\leq L_{D}^{\star}+\min_{j}\delta_{j}\leq L_{D}^{\star}+\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}L_{j}^{\star}\leq(1+1/d)L_{D}^{\star}.

The uniform coordinate pairs (ej,0),(ej,2)(e_{j},0),(e_{j},2) attain equality, giving Γd​(2​d−1)=1+1/d\Gamma_{d}(2d-1)=1+1/d for every d≥1d\geq 1. All upper bounds here are attained by explicit selections.

The equality analysis is stronger than the value alone: every extremizer has maximal certificate complexity, zero zero-feature loss, equal positive block losses, factor-two extremal blocks, and lower bounds on all canonical rank-deficient projection selections. The complete necessary conditions, one-dimensional profile, and instance-dependent bound remain in Theorems 11–13. These are necessary extremal conditions, not an asserted sufficient classification of every boundary extremizer.

6 Conclusion

The exact law Γd​(n)=3−n/d\Gamma_{d}(n)=3-n/d holds throughout the upper-half interval, with a complete Lean 4 verification of its dataset-level statement. Balanced anchors, positive-weight lifting, and independent-line compression close the dimension induction. At (5,6)(5,6), the separate circuit analysis proves the block prediction 11/511/5 for arbitrary configurations. These results connect dimension-uniform budget laws with the finer geometry needed below the upper-half interval.

Reproducibility statement

Appendices A and B contain complete proofs, including zero residuals, deficient ranks, and positive-weight limits. Appendix E maps the supplied symbolic checker to the algebra it tests and gives reproduction commands. The checker verifies the stated finite algebraic identities. Appendix C gives the upper-half proof and its Lean 4 theorem map; the supplied formal project checks the full statement and its foundational dependencies. Appendix D proves the block frontier and gives the matrix formulation for further intermediate budgets.

Appendix A Full certificate statements and boundary proofs

A.1 Exact certificates and intrinsic-rank rigidity

For a selection q∈ΔNq\in\Delta_{N}, let Lq​(w)=∑i=1Nqi​(⟨w,xi⟩−yi)2L_{q}(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_{i}(\langle w,x_{i}\rangle-y_{i})^{2} denote the selected objective, and write

Uq=span⁡{xi:qi>0},h⁡(q)=∑i=1Nqi​gi.U_{q}=\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:q_{i}>0\},\qquad h(q)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}q_{i}g_{i}.

The quantities have distinct roles: h⁡(q)h(q) is the selected half-gradient at the full-data solution, so ∇Lq​(w⋆)=2​h​(q)\nabla L_{q}(w^{\star})=2h(q), whereas UqU_{q} determines the minimum-norm tie-breaking rule.

Theorem 7 (Exact-Selection Certificate Theorem).

For every q∈ΔNq\in\Delta_{N},

w^(q)=w⋆⟺h(q)=0andw⋆∈Uq.\widehat{w}(q)=w^{\star}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(q)=0\ \text{and}\ w^{\star}\in U_{q}. (A.1)

In particular, the full-observed-span conditions

h⁡(q)=0,Uq=Uh(q)=0,\qquad U_{q}=U (A.2)

imply w^​(q)=w⋆\widehat{w}(q)=w^{\star} and LD​(w^​(q))=LD⋆L_{D}(\widehat{w}(q))=L_{D}^{\star}.

Proof.

The selected objective depends only on the projection of ww onto UqU_{q}, so its minimum-norm minimizer belongs to UqU_{q}. Consequently, w^​(q)=w⋆\widehat{w}(q)=w^{\star} implies w⋆∈Uqw^{\star}\in U_{q}. Stationarity at w⋆w^{\star} also gives 0=∇Lq​(w⋆)=2​h​(q)0=\nabla L_{q}(w^{\star})=2h(q), proving necessity.

Conversely, if h⁡(q)=0h(q)=0, then w⋆w^{\star} minimizes the selected convex quadratic. Because all weights on supp⁡(q)\operatorname{supp}(q) are positive, its Hessian has kernel Uq⟂U_{q}^{\perp}, and the complete minimizer set is w⋆+Uq⟂w^{\star}+U_{q}^{\perp}. If w⋆∈Uqw^{\star}\in U_{q}, it is orthogonal to this kernel and is therefore the unique minimum-norm point of the affine minimizer set. Finally, w⋆∈Uw^{\star}\in U by the full-data minimum-norm convention, so Equation A.2 is sufficient. ∎

The full-span condition yields a geometric certificate complexity controlled by intrinsic rank.

Definition 8 (Full-span certificate complexity).

The full-span certificate complexity of DD is

κ(D)=min{|supp(q)|:q∈ΔN,h(q)=0,Uq=U}.\kappa(D)=\min\left\{|\operatorname{supp}(q)|:q\in\Delta_{N},\ h(q)=0,\ U_{q}=U\right\}. (A.3)

The feasible set is nonempty because the original weights pp satisfy Equation 14 and have feature span UU. Since support sizes take values in the finite set {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\}, the displayed minimum is attained.

The first complexity bound depends on the observed rank and the intrinsic dimension of the nonzero gradient atoms rather than on the ambient dimension alone.

Theorem 9 (Intrinsic-Dimension Certificate Bound).

Let

m=dimU,V=span⁡{gi:gi≠0},r=dimV.m=\dim U,\qquad V=\operatorname{span}\{g_{i}:g_{i}\neq 0\},\qquad r=\dim V.

If m=0m=0, then κ⁡(D)=1\kappa(D)=1. If m≥1m\geq 1, then

m≤κ⁡(D)≤m+r≤2​m≤2​d.m\leq\kappa(D)\leq m+r\leq 2m\leq 2d. (A.4)

In particular, r<mr<m implies κ⁡(D)≤2​m−1\kappa(D)\leq 2m-1, and 1≤m<d1\leq m<d implies κ⁡(D)≤2​d−2\kappa(D)\leq 2d-2.

The proof first compresses the active gradient balance to at most 2​r2r atoms by Steinitz’s theorem and then adds at most m−rm-r zero-gradient features to complete the observed span. Assume m=dimU≥1m=\dim U\geq 1. Then the following statements are equivalent.

    κ⁡(D)=2​m\kappa(D)=2m.

For the forward direction, Theorem 9 first forces the active gradients to span UU. For a full-dimensional interior subset BB, relative interior gives pos⁡(B)=U\operatorname{pos}(B)=U. Thus BB is inclusion-minimal, and κ⁡(D)=2​m\kappa(D)=2m forces the maximal positive-basis size 2​m2m, so BB consists of opposite pairs. For the converse, a spanning certificate must represent every independent line, and balance on a line cannot use only one nonzero gradient; hence it needs at least two points per line. The full proof, including the positive coefficients, zero features, and m=1m=1, is in A.6.

A.3 Instance-dependent and sharp boundary laws

The certificate complexity separates instances admitting a full-span exact certificate at budget 2​d−12d-1 from the maximal-complexity branch that requires additional control. On the latter branch, Theorem 11 supplies an explicit one-point compression bound with a data-dependent penalty before any worst-case averaging is used.

Theorem 12 (Instance-Dependent Penultimate-Budget Bound).

For every finite weighted regression instance in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, exactly one of the following two alternatives holds.

    If κ⁡(D)≤2​d−1\kappa(D)\leq 2d-1, then

In the second case,

LD⋆​(2​d−1,A⋆)≤LD⋆+minj⁡δj≤LD⋆+minj⁡Lj⋆≤LD⋆+1d​∑j=1dLj⋆≤(1+1d)​LD⋆.L_{D}^{\star}(2d-1;A^{\star})\leq L_{D}^{\star}+\min_{j}\delta_{j}\leq L_{D}^{\star}+\min_{j}L_{j}^{\star}\leq L_{D}^{\star}+\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}L_{j}^{\star}\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{d}\right)L_{D}^{\star}. (A.18)
Proof.

Theorem 9 gives κ⁡(D)≤2​d\kappa(D)\leq 2d, so the two integer-valued alternatives are exhaustive and disjoint. In case (a), a minimizing certificate in Equation A.3 is a feasible selection with at most 2​d−12d-1 support points. Theorem 7 recovers w⋆w^{\star}. Since LD⋆L_{D}^{\star} is the minimum of the original risk over all predictors, the selected infimum equals the full optimum.

In case (b), Theorem 10 gives U=ℝdU=\mathbb{R}^{d} and the decomposition

LD⋆=C0+∑j=1dLj⋆.L_{D}^{\star}=C_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}L_{j}^{\star}.

Choose j0j_{0} minimizing δj\delta_{j}. Use the two-point exact compression from Theorem 11 on every line j≠j0j\neq j_{0}, and use the best one-point compression on line j0j_{0}. The implementation following Equation A.15 gives a genuine regression selection with positive weights and at most 2​(d−1)+1=2​d−12(d-1)+1=2d-1 support points. Its original-data risk is exactly

C0+∑j=1dLj⋆+δj0=LD⋆+minj⁡δj,C_{0}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}L_{j}^{\star}+\delta_{j_{0}}=L_{D}^{\star}+\min_{j}\delta_{j},

The universal factor is sharp. Equality in the universal bound forces equality at every stage of Equation A.18 together with lower bounds for every canonical rank-deficient projection selection.

Theorem 13 (Sharp Boundary Law and Extremal Rigidity).

For every integer d≥1d\geq 1,

Γd​(2​d−1)=1+1d.\boxed{\Gamma_{d}(2d-1)=1+\frac{1}{d}.} (A.19)

LD⋆​(2​d−1,A⋆)LD⋆=1+1d.\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(2d-1;A^{\star})}{L_{D}^{\star}}=1+\frac{1}{d}. (A.20)

12​d​(tj2+(tj−2)2)=1d+(tj−1)2d.\frac{1}{2d}\bigl(t_{j}^{2}+(t_{j}-2)^{2}\bigr)=\frac{1}{d}+\frac{(t_{j}-1)^{2}}{d}. (A.25)

A.4 Convex-geometric preliminaries

We record the two external convex-geometric inputs and the positivity facts used below. If a finite set GG spans a linear space VV and zero is a strictly positive convex combination of all points in GG, then

0∈relintV⁡conv⁡(G).0\in\operatorname{relint}_{V}\operatorname{conv}(G).

Indeed, a supporting functional at zero would be nonnegative on GG. Applying it to the strictly positive combination forces it to vanish on every point of GG, and hence on VV, a contradiction. Conversely, if 0∈relint⁡conv⁡(G)0\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}(G), then zero has a convex representation with a strictly positive coefficient on every point of GG. This is the standard identity that a linear map sends the relative interior of a simplex onto the relative interior of its image.

Carathéodory’s theorem gives a small convex representation, but such a representation need not retain the full-dimensional relative-interior property required here Scherk (1966).

We use Steinitz’s theorem in the following relative-interior form: if zero is in the relative interior of the convex hull of a finite subset of an rr-dimensional linear space, then a subset of at most 2​r2r points still has an rr-dimensional convex hull containing zero in its relative interior Steinitz (1916); Ivanov & Naszódi (2024).

We also use the extremal structure of a positive basis. An inclusion-minimal positive spanning set in an mm-dimensional space has at most 2​m2m vectors; if it has exactly 2​m2m, then, after rescaling and reindexing, it is

{ajvj,−bjvj:j∈[m]},aj,bj>0,\{a_{j}v_{j},-b_{j}v_{j}:j\in[m]\},\qquad a_{j},b_{j}>0,

for a basis v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m}. This is the maximal-cardinality case of the positive-basis structure theorem; see Davis (1954); Regis (2016) and the discussion preceding Theorem 2 of Nævdal (2019).

Proof of Theorem 9.

Because gig_{i} is a scalar multiple of xix_{i}, V⊆UV\subseteq U, and hence r≤mr\leq m. If m=0m=0, all features and gradients are zero. Any one-point selection is a full-span certificate, while every point of ΔN\Delta_{N} has nonempty support. Thus κ⁡(D)=1\kappa(D)=1.

Assume m≥1m\geq 1. Every collection of features spanning UU contains at least mm points, so κ⁡(D)≥m\kappa(D)\geq m. If r=0r=0, all gradients are zero. Choose mm features forming a basis of UU and give them arbitrary positive normalized weights. This is a certificate with mm points, so the claimed upper bound holds.

It remains to consider r≥1r\geq 1. Let

A={i:gi≠0}.A=\{i:g_{i}\neq 0\}.

The active gradients span VV. By Equation 14, positivity of the original masses, and gi=0g_{i}=0 outside AA,

∑i∈Api​gi=0.\sum_{i\in A}p_{i}g_{i}=0.

If r<mr<m, the active features span exactly VV. Select a set Z⊆[N]∖AZ\subseteq[N]\setminus A of m−rm-r indices whose feature cosets form a basis of U/VU/V. Every z∈Zz\in Z has gz=0g_{z}=0. qi=(1−ε)​βi(i∈T),qz=ε​ηz(z∈Z),q_{i}=(1-\varepsilon)\beta_{i}\quad(i\in T),\qquad q_{z}=\varepsilon\eta_{z}\quad(z\in Z),

with all other weights zero. Its gradient sum is zero, its features span UU, and its support size is at most

A.6 Proof of maximal certificate-complexity rigidity

Proof of Theorem 10.

Assume first that κ⁡(D)=2​m\kappa(D)=2m. Theorem 9 gives 2​m≤m+r≤2​m2m\leq m+r\leq 2m, so r=mr=m and V=UV=U. As in the preceding proof, the positive full-data balance puts zero in the relative interior of the convex hull of the active gradients. Steinitz’s theorem supplies a full-dimensional interior subset BB of at most 2​m2m active gradients. Its strictly positive balancing coefficients and its feature span make it a certificate. Moreover,

0∈relintU⁡conv⁡(B)⟹pos⁡(B)=U,0\in\operatorname{relint}_{U}\operatorname{conv}(B)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{pos}(B)=U,

because a relative neighborhood of zero in UU lies in conv⁡(B)\operatorname{conv}(B). If a proper subset C⊂BC\subset B positively spanned UU, then −c∈pos⁡(C)-c\in\operatorname{pos}(C) for every c∈Cc\in C. Summing these representations would give a zero combination with a strictly positive coefficient on every point of CC. After normalization, these coefficients would balance the corresponding active gradients. Because every active gradient is a nonzero scalar multiple of its feature, the corresponding features also span UU. Thus CC would yield a smaller full-span certificate. Maximality of κ⁡(D)\kappa(D) rules this out and also forces |B|=2​m|B|=2m. Hence BB is an inclusion-minimal positive spanning set of maximal cardinality. By the structure theorem in A.4, after reindexing,

B={ajvj,−bjvj:j∈[m]},aj,bj>0,B=\{a_{j}v_{j},-b_{j}v_{j}:j\in[m]\},\qquad a_{j},b_{j}>0, (A.26)

for a basis v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m} of UU.

We next rule out a mixed active gradient. Suppose an active gradient outside the union of the basis lines has the expansion

h=∑j∈Jcj​vj,|J|≥2,cj≠0.h=\sum_{j\in J}c_{j}v_{j},\qquad|J|\geq 2,\qquad c_{j}\neq 0.

Give hh coefficient one. For each j∈Jj\in J, choose from Equation A.26 the vector with sign opposite to cjc_{j}, with the unique positive coefficient that cancels cj​vjc_{j}v_{j}. For each k∉Jk\notin J, choose both vectors of the kkth pair with positive coefficients that balance the pair. The resulting positive combination sums to zero, spans UU, and uses

active points. After normalization it is a smaller certificate, a contradiction. Hence every active gradient, and therefore its feature, lies on one of the lines ℝ​vj\mathbb{R}v_{j}.

Now suppose that an index ℓ\ell has xℓ≠0x_{\ell}\neq 0 but gℓ=0g_{\ell}=0. Write xℓ=∑jcj​vjx_{\ell}=\sum_{j}c_{j}v_{j} and choose kk with ck≠0c_{k}\neq 0. Select ℓ\ell and both members of every pair in Equation A.26 except the kkth pair. Give the pairs positive balancing coefficients and give ℓ\ell any positive coefficient. The gradients balance, while xℓx_{\ell} together with {vj:j≠k}\{v_{j}:j\neq k\} spans UU. This certificate uses 1+2​(m−1)=2​m−11+2(m-1)=2m-1 points, again a contradiction. Thus every nonzero feature has a nonzero gradient, proving the geometric condition in (ii).

Conversely, assume (ii). For each line write every gradient on that line as gi=γi​vjg_{i}=\gamma_{i}v_{j}, where γi≠0\gamma_{i}\neq 0. Each line is represented because the features span UU. Resolving the full-data balance Equation 14 in the basis v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m} gives

B.4 Systems whose positive circuits have rank at most two

Assume now that every positive circuit has rank at most two. A circuit plane is the span of an actual positive triangle, that is, a rank-two positive circuit. We use the following elementary observation repeatedly. A support-minimal nonnegative representation of a nonzero vector has independent positive support: otherwise a dependence permits a coefficient perturbation until one coefficient vanishes. If two such representations give opposite directions in subspaces intersecting in a line, their union has exactly one dependence and is a positive circuit.

Lemma 19 (Intersecting circuit planes).

The following statements hold.

  1. 1.

    Two distinct circuit planes with a nonzero intersection share the same oriented vertex direction in any chosen witnessing triangles.

  2. 2.

    A family of distinct circuit planes in a three-space, with no common line, contains at most three planes.

  3. 3.

    Distinct circuit planes sharing a line have independent directions in the quotient by that line.

  4. 4.

    A circuit plane has zero intersection with at most two members of a family of distinct circuit planes sharing a line.

Proof.

For the first assertion, take z≠0z\neq 0 on the intersection line and support-minimal positive representations of z,−zz,-z in each triangle. Within each triangle their support sizes sum to at least three, since a positive triangle contains no opposite parallel pair. The two cross-paired representations each form a circuit, with at most three roots. Adding the two inequalities forces both within-triangle sums to equal three. Each triangle therefore has a singleton representation of one direction. These directions must agree; if they opposed one another, the other cross-pair would contain four roots.

For the second assertion, choose three planes with no common line. Their pairwise intersection directions are independent; by the first assertion, the witnessing triangles can be written, after positive scaling, as

{u,v,−a​u−b​v},{u,w,−c​u−d​w},{v,w,−e​v−f​w},a,b,c,d,e,f>0.\{u,v,-au-bv\},\quad\{u,w,-cu-dw\},\quad\{v,w,-ev-fw\},\qquad a,b,c,d,e,f>0.

A fourth plane containing none of the axes would have to contain all three negative edge directions. Their determinant has absolute value a​d​e+b​c​f>0ade+bcf>0, which excludes a plane. If the fourth plane contains uu, it contains neither vv nor ww. Its intersection with the third plane must be the direction −e​v−f​w-ev-fw, so its third triangle root has the form g=−α​u+β​e​v+β​f​wg=-\alpha u+\beta ev+\beta fw, α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0. But

g+β​eb​(−a​u−b​v)+β​fd​(−c​u−d​w)+(α+β​e​ab+β​f​cd)​u=0g+\frac{\beta e}{b}(-au-bv)+\frac{\beta f}{d}(-cu-dw)+\left(\alpha+\frac{\beta ea}{b}+\frac{\beta fc}{d}\right)u=0

is a rank-three positive circuit. The other axes are symmetric.

For the third assertion, the first part gives a common oriented root uu. Normalize each triangle to u+xi+yi=0u+x_{i}+y_{i}=0, and write xi=ei−u/2x_{i}=e_{i}-u/2, yi=−ei−u/2y_{i}=-e_{i}-u/2. A minimal dependence of their quotient directions would be ∑i=1kti​ei=c​u\sum_{i=1}^{k}t_{i}e_{i}=cu, with ti≠0t_{i}\neq 0, k≥3k\geq 3. Put S=∑i|ti|S=\sum_{i}|t_{i}|. The two choices of signed leaf directions give positive combinations equal to (c−S/2)​u(c-S/2)u and (−c−S/2)​u(-c-S/2)u. At least one coefficient is negative. Adding a positive multiple of uu gives a rank-kk circuit, by minimality of the quotient dependence, a contradiction.

For the last assertion, take three shared-line planes Qi=span⁡(u,ei)Q_{i}=\operatorname{span}(u,e_{i}); their sum WW has dimension four. Their seven-root core consists of uu and ±ei−u/2\pm e_{i}-u/2. Suppose a circuit plane PP is disjoint from every QiQ_{i}. If P⊄WP\not\subset W, then P∩WP\cap W is a line containing no core root direction. Both signs of that direction need at least two core roots, and at least one sign needs two roots in the triangle spanning PP. Cross-pairing gives a circuit of rank at least three. If P⊂WP\subset W, write a triangle root as p=z0​u+∑i=13zi​eip=z_{0}u+\sum_{i=1}^{3}z_{i}e_{i}. It has at least two nonzero leaf coordinates, since P∩Qi=0P\cap Q_{i}=0. A minimal core representation of −p-p must have exactly two parents to avoid a higher-rank circuit. They are leaves of different arms, forcing z0=(|zi|+|zj|)/2>0z_{0}=(|z_{i}|+|z_{j}|)/2>0. This holds for all three roots of the triangle spanning PP, contradicting their positive zero relation. ∎

Let GG be the finite simple graph whose vertices are the distinct circuit planes, with an edge exactly when two planes have zero intersection.

Lemma 20 (Short cycles give a four-plus-one decomposition).

If GG has a triangle or a four-cycle, every root lies in W∪LW\cup L for a four-space WW and a complementary line LL. In this case δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1.

Proof.

For a graph triangle, the first two planes span a four-space WW. If the third plane lay outside it, their intersection line would contain no root of the first two witnessing triangles, by pairwise disjointness. Its two signs need at least two roots from that core, and at least one sign needs two from the third triangle. Their cross-pair gives a circuit of rank at least three. Thus all three planes lie in WW.

A chorded four-cycle contains a triangle. For an induced four-cycle, write its parts as A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} and B1,B2B_{1},B_{2}, and put U=A1+A2U=A_{1}+A_{2}, V=B1+B2V=B_{1}+B_{2}. These are three-spaces. If their sum had dimension five, their intersection would be a line. Each side has a positive generating core formed by two triangles with a same-oriented shared vertex, and hence no opposite parallel roots. For a direction on the intersection line, the minimal representation sizes of its two signs sum to at least three on either side. Cross-pairing produces two circuits, each with at most three roots. Equality is forced in both sums, so each side has a singleton representation. The intersection line would then lie in some AiA_{i} and some BjB_{j}, contradicting a cross-edge. The four planes therefore lie in a four-space WW.

Consider any other circuit plane D⊄WD\not\subset W. In the triangle case it meets at most one original plane nontrivially; with the other two it gives a triangle spanning five dimensions. In the four-cycle case, if it meets at most one original plane, choose an adjacent pair among the other three and obtain the same contradiction. If it meets two, they must belong to one part of the cycle, and it meets neither plane of the other part. Replacing one plane of the first part by DD gives an induced four-cycle spanning five dimensions. Thus every circuit plane is in WW.

Every root outside WW must now belong to a rank-one circuit and therefore has a root on its opposite ray. If two distinct exterior lines occurred, choose roots on them with opposite quotient directions modulo WW. Their positive combination gives a nonzero z∈Wz\in W. A minimal positive representation of −z-z in the core of WW, combined with these two exterior roots, gives a circuit of rank at least two containing an exterior root. This contradicts the preceding result. Thus all exterior roots lie on one complementary line LL.

Let the evaluation masses in W,LW,L be a,b>0a,b>0, a+b=1a+b=1. Mean zero splits along this direct sum. Their two positive semidefinite second moments have ranks four and one and sum to I5I_{5}; their complementary ranges are therefore orthogonal, and the moments are the orthogonal projections. In the conditional four-dimensional system, scaling the roots by a\sqrt{a} gives unit covariance. The four-dimensional five-row theorem of (Zhang, 2026, Theorem 47) then gives an excess infimum at most aa in the original coordinates. On LL, interpolate a root of greatest absolute coefficient to give excess at most bb. Combining the two full-rank fits uses at most six rows and gives excess at most a+b=1a+b=1. The positive-weight form of the four-dimensional input is justified in Subsection B.6 below. ∎

In the remaining case GG has no triangles or four-cycles. Neighbors of a vertex are pairwise intersecting planes. Such a plane family either shares a line or lies in a three-space. Indeed, two planes span a three-space SS and meet in a line ℓ\ell. A third meeting both without containing ℓ\ell lies in SS. A plane outside SS meeting the first two would have to contain ℓ\ell, and could then not meet that third plane. This proves the dichotomy. Lemma 19 bounds the first case by two neighbors and the second by three. Consequently Δ⁡(G)≤3\Delta(G)\leq 3.

Lemma 21 (A graph probability).

Every nonempty finite graph with no triangles or four-cycles and maximum degree at most three has a vertex probability θ\theta such that

∑A∼BθA−θB≤15for every vertex ​B.\sum_{A\sim B}\theta_{A}-\theta_{B}\leq\frac{1}{5}\quad\hbox{for every vertex }B. (B.20)
Proof.

If a vertex has degree three, assign it mass 2/52/5 and its three neighbors mass 1/51/5 each. The left side is 1/51/5 on this star. An exterior vertex meets at most one positive-mass neighbor, since two would create a four-cycle, and it does not meet the center. If the maximum degree is at most two, choose one component. On a cycle of length m≥5m\geq 5, use the uniform probability. For paths on one, two, three, and four vertices, respectively use

(1),(1/2,1/2),(2/7,3/7,2/7),(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6).(1),\quad(1/2,1/2),\quad(2/7,3/7,2/7),\quad(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6).

Their left sides have maxima −1,0,1/7,1/6-1,0,1/7,1/6, respectively. For a longer path put mass 1/51/5 on each of five consecutive vertices. Every vertex, including those immediately outside the segment, satisfies (B.20). All other components have zero mass. ∎

Choose one actual triangle for each graph vertex as an anchor. For any rank-two circuit BB, set

ρA​B=2−dim(PA∩PB)=1+𝟏A∼B−𝟏PA=PB.\rho_{AB}=2-\dim(P_{A}\cap P_{B})=1+\boldsymbol{1}_{A\sim B}-\boldsymbol{1}_{P_{A}=P_{B}}.

For a rank-one circuit, set ρA​B=1−dim(PA∩PB)≤1\rho_{AB}=1-\dim(P_{A}\cap P_{B})\leq 1. Equation (B.20) gives ∑AθA​ρA​B≤6/5\sum_{A}\theta_{A}\rho_{AB}\leq 6/5 for every rank-two circuit.

We now convert this inequality to the original evaluation risk. For a fixed anchor AA, the polytope

𝒫A={z∈PA⟂:vi⊤​z≤1​ for all ​i}\mathcal{P}_{A}=\{z\in P_{A}^{\perp}:v_{i}^{\top}z\leq 1\text{ for all }i\}

is bounded, three-dimensional, and contains zero in its interior. Express zero as a convex combination of its vertices. Each vertex has three active roots independent modulo PAP_{A}. These interpolating roots and the zero-evaluation triangle anchor produce an actual positive-weight full-rank six-row fit.

Fix a positive circuit BB, with normalized coefficients βi>0\beta_{i}>0, ∑i∈Bβi=1\sum_{i\in B}\beta_{i}=1. Project it modulo PAP_{A}, discard zero projections, and let their remaining coefficient mass be mA​B≤1m_{AB}\leq 1. Decompose the resulting positive zero relation into normalized projected circuits. Their mixing masses sum to mA​Bm_{AB}, and their ranks are at most ρA​B\rho_{AB}. For one such circuit with coefficients αi\alpha_{i} and support size ss, set Ti=vi⊤​zT_{i}=v_{i}^{\top}z under the mean-zero vertex distribution. Then Ti≤1T_{i}\leq 1, ∑iαi​Ti=0\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}T_{i}=0 pointwise, and 𝔼​Ti=0\mathbb{E}T_{i}=0. Hence

−(1−αi)/αi≤Ti≤1,𝔼Ti2≤(1−αi)/αi.-(1-\alpha_{i})/\alpha_{i}\leq T_{i}\leq 1,\qquad\mathbb{E}T_{i}^{2}\leq(1-\alpha_{i})/\alpha_{i}.

The second inequality follows by averaging (Ti+(1−αi)/αi)​(Ti−1)≤0(T_{i}+(1-\alpha_{i})/\alpha_{i})(T_{i}-1)\leq 0. Thus 𝔼​∑iαi​Ti2≤s−1≤ρA​B\mathbb{E}\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}T_{i}^{2}\leq s-1\leq\rho_{AB}. Reassemble the projected circuits to obtain

𝔼A​∑i∈Bβi​(vi⊤​z)2≤mA​B​ρA​B≤ρA​B.\mathbb{E}_{A}\sum_{i\in B}\beta_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}z)^{2}\leq m_{AB}\rho_{AB}\leq\rho_{AB}. (B.21)

Finally mix anchors according to θ\theta, and decompose the original mean-zero probability λ\lambda into normalized positive circuits. Use (B.21), the graph bound for rank-two circuits, and the bound one for rank-one circuits. The original covariance gives

𝔼​‖z‖2=𝔼​∑iλi​(vi⊤​z)2≤65.\mathbb{E}\|z\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}(v_{i}^{\top}z)^{2}\leq\frac{6}{5}. (B.22)

These are finite distributions on actual fits, so some fit satisfies the same bound.

If there are no circuit planes, every root has an opposite root, and their distinct unoriented lines are independent. Otherwise a minimal line dependence, oriented using the available opposite roots, would give a positive circuit of rank at least two. There are therefore five independent lines; choose a maximum-absolute-coefficient root on each and interpolate. All evaluations have absolute value at most one. This also gives δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1, and completes the low-rank case.

B.5 The remaining rank-three case and the global root bound

Suppose that a rank-three circuit AA exists, that every circuit has rank at most three, and that the configuration (B.6) is absent. First suppose that no seven roots positively generate ℝ5\mathbb{R}^{5}. In the two-dimensional quotient by PAP_{A}, a positive generating triangle would lift, together with the four anchor roots, to a seven-root positive generating set. A planar positive generating system with no such triangle lies on two independent lines: a minimal positive basis consists of two opposite pairs, and any root off their axes would form a positive triangle with two suitably oriented axis roots. Choosing maximum-absolute-coefficient roots on these quotient lines, and interpolating with zero anchor evaluations, gives δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1.

Otherwise choose a minimal positive generating subset of seven roots. It has exactly seven roots, since a six-root positive generating set in dimension five would be a rank-five circuit. Its relation space has dimension two, and its nonnegative relation cone is full-dimensional and pointed in that space, with two extreme rays. Their circuit supports cover the seven roots and each has at most four roots. The possibilities are disjoint supports of sizes four and three, or two four-root supports sharing one root. The latter is (B.6), already excluded. The former gives complementary spaces U,WU,W of dimensions three and two, with normalized relations

a0+a1+a2+a3=0,b0+b1+b2=0,U⊕W=ℝ5.a_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}=0,\qquad b_{0}+b_{1}+b_{2}=0,\qquad U\oplus W=\mathbb{R}^{5}. (B.23)

For a crossing exceptional root gg, write −g-g as a nonnegative combination in each simplex with minimum coefficient zero. If the positive support sizes are p,q≥1p,q\geq 1, their union is independent; avoiding a high-rank circuit forces p+q≤3p+q\leq 3. For (1,1)(1,1), the complementary three A and two B roots positively generate gg, making it good. For (1,2)(1,2), unequal B coefficients again make gg good, while equal coefficients give g=−α​ai+β​bkg=-\alpha a_{i}+\beta b_{k}. Together with aia_{i} and the other two B roots this is a rank-three circuit sharing aia_{i} with the original A circuit and jointly spanning dimension five, a forbidden shared-vertex configuration. For (2,1)(2,1), unequal A coefficients likewise make gg good, so the remaining form is

g=−α⁡(ai+aj)−β​bk,α,β>0.g=-\alpha(a_{i}+a_{j})-\beta b_{k},\qquad\alpha,\beta>0. (B.24)

It gives a rank-three circuit with span span⁡(ai,aj,bk)\operatorname{span}(a_{i},a_{j},b_{k}).

Encode these roots in a bipartite graph. The three unordered two-plus-two partitions of the four A indices form one side, and the three B indices form the other. Two edges disjoint on both sides would have A pairs sharing exactly one index. Their two circuits would share that real A root and span five dimensions, again giving (B.6). Thus the occupied edges pairwise intersect and form a star. Choose one crossing circuit as anchor. If the A partition is fixed, every crossing A component is zero in its quotient, including the complementary pair because the four A roots sum to zero. If the B index is fixed, every crossing B component is zero there. Both original blocks project onto independent lines. In either case, all exceptional projections lie on these two lines, giving δ6≤1\delta_{6}\leq 1. If there are no crossing exceptional roots, the (3,2)(3,2) cover in (B.4) gives δ6≤6/5\delta_{6}\leq 6/5.

The cases now exhaust all root systems: ranks four and five were handled in Subsection B.1, the shared-vertex case in Subsection B.3, and ranks at most two in Subsection B.4. Therefore every finite normalized root system satisfies

δ6​(V)≤65.\delta_{6}(V)\leq\frac{6}{5}. (B.25)

B.6 Transfer to the original weighted regression problem

We use the four-dimensional five-point upper bound two from (Zhang, 2026, Theorem 47), including its construction by strictly convex finite training problems or limits of such problems. Its uniform-evaluation statement extends to strictly positive evaluation weights as follows. Approximate them by positive rational probabilities on the same support, and duplicate rows to obtain uniform datasets. Duplicate selected rows can be merged without increasing support. The set of full-rank training outputs is independent of evaluation weights. The evaluation covariance has a uniform positive lower eigenvalue near the original weights, so bounded-risk selected outputs are bounded. The changes in their evaluation risks consequently tend to zero uniformly on this bounded set, as does the change in the optimal risk. Taking infima proves the weighted statement.

For observed feature rank four, apply that input after an isometric restriction. For rank three use the five-point boundary theorem already proved in this paper; ranks at most two admit full-span exact recovery with at most four points. The zero-optimal-risk case was settled in the problem formulation. It remains to consider rank five and L⋆>0L^{\star}>0.

Set

H=∑ipixixi⊤≻0,ξi=H−1/2xi,ηi=yi−xi⊤​w⋆L⋆,z=H1/2​(w−w⋆)L⋆.H=\sum_{i}p_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\succ 0,\quad\xi_{i}=H^{-1/2}x_{i},\quad\eta_{i}=\frac{y_{i}-x_{i}^{\top}w^{\star}}{\sqrt{L^{\star}}},\quad z=\frac{H^{1/2}(w-w^{\star})}{\sqrt{L^{\star}}}.

Then

∑ipi​ξi​ξi⊤=I5,∑ipi​ηi​ξi=0,∑ipi​ηi2=1,LD​(w)L⋆=1+‖z‖2.\sum_{i}p_{i}\xi_{i}\xi_{i}^{\top}=I_{5},\quad\sum_{i}p_{i}\eta_{i}\xi_{i}=0,\quad\sum_{i}p_{i}\eta_{i}^{2}=1,\quad\frac{L_{D}(w)}{L^{\star}}=1+\|z\|^{2}. (B.26)

Every full-rank training problem has a unique solution, so the invertible change of coordinates respects the original minimum-norm learner.

If some row has η0=0\eta_{0}=0, ξ0≠0\xi_{0}\neq 0, project the regression problem onto ξ0⟂\xi_{0}^{\perp}. Its covariance is the identity on this four-space, its optimum is zero, and its optimal risk is one. The four-dimensional input provides a strictly convex training objective FF on at most five projected rows, whose constrained minimizer has squared norm at most 1+ϵ1+\epsilon. Lift those rows and add row zero with weight M>0M>0, giving F⁡(z)+M​(ξ0⊤​z)2F(z)+M(\xi_{0}^{\top}z)^{2}. Its Hessian is positive definite since FF is strictly convex on ξ0⟂\xi_{0}^{\perp}. As M→∞M\to\infty, its unique solution converges to the constrained solution. This follows also by taking the Schur complement in the normal equations relative to ξ0⟂\xi_{0}^{\perp} and its normal line. Each finite MM uses at most six rows with positive weights. Letting M→∞M\to\infty and then ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0 gives risk-ratio infimum at most two.

We may therefore assume ηi=0\eta_{i}=0 implies ξi=0\xi_{i}=0. For ηi≠0\eta_{i}\neq 0, put vi=ξi/ηiv_{i}=\xi_{i}/\eta_{i} and λi=pi​ηi2\lambda_{i}=p_{i}\eta_{i}^{2}. Remove the zero roots, corresponding to pure-residual rows, and write a∈(0,1]a\in(0,1] for the mass of the remaining roots. Their mean is zero and their second moment is I5I_{5}. The rescaled system v~i=a​vi\widetilde{v}_{i}=\sqrt{a}\,v_{i}, λ~i=λi/a\widetilde{\lambda}_{i}=\lambda_{i}/a satisfies (B.1). Equation (B.25) gives a sequence of six-row full-rank positive-weight outputs, and z=a​z~z=\sqrt{a}\,\widetilde{z} gives

inf‖z‖2≤a​65≤65.\inf\|z\|^{2}\leq a\frac{6}{5}\leq\frac{6}{5}.

Convert each root training weight wiw_{i} to the original sample weight wi/ηi2w_{i}/\eta_{i}^{2}, and normalize all selected weights by their sum. The selected objective changes only by a positive common factor; support, positivity, and full rank are preserved. Thus

Γ5​(6)≤115.\Gamma_{5}(6)\leq\frac{11}{5}. (B.27)

Let

x0=e1,x1=e2,x2=e3,x3=−e1−e2−e3,x4=e4,x5=e5,x6=−e4−e5.x_{0}=e_{1},\quad x_{1}=e_{2},\quad x_{2}=e_{3},\quad x_{3}=-e_{1}-e_{2}-e_{3},\qquad x_{4}=e_{4},\quad x_{5}=e_{5},\quad x_{6}=-e_{4}-e_{5}.

h=(10,20,40,80,160)⊤,yi=xi⊤​h+1.h=(10,20,40,80,160)^{\top},\qquad y_{i}=x_{i}^{\top}h+1.

M=diag⁡(110​(I3+𝟏𝟏⊤),15​(I2+𝟏𝟏⊤)),M=\operatorname{diag}\left(\tfrac{1}{10}(I_{3}+\boldsymbol{1}\boldsymbol{1}^{\top}),\tfrac{1}{5}(I_{2}+\boldsymbol{1}\boldsymbol{1}^{\top})\right),

The other block has nonnegative excess. Equality is attained by taking all four A rows with equal training weights, giving zero block displacement, and any two B rows, which interpolate.

For a rank-deficient selection, the minimum-norm solution lies in its selected feature span. min⁡{100,400,1600,(20−10)2/2,(40−10)2/2,(40−20)2/2}=50.\min\{100,400,1600,(20-10)^{2}/2,(40-10)^{2}/2,(40-20)^{2}/2\}=50.

min⁡{802,1602,(160−80)2/2}=3200.\min\{80^{2},160^{2},(160-80)^{2}/2\}=3200.

Appendix C Complete proof of the upper-half law

This appendix proves Theorem 1. Throughout, training weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and only their positive entries count toward the support. All limits below preserve the selected feature span at every positive mixture parameter.

C.1 Certificates and positive spanning sets

Set gi=(xi⊤​w⋆−yi)​xig_{i}=(x_{i}^{\top}w^{\star}-y_{i})x_{i}. The full normal equation is ∑ipi​gi=0\sum_{i}p_{i}g_{i}=0. A nonempty support BB is a full-span certificate if its features span UU and some strictly positive coefficients on BB balance the gig_{i}. Normalizing those coefficients gives an admissible selection returning w⋆w^{\star}. Indeed, the selected and full minimizer sets are both w⋆+U⟂w^{\star}+U^{\perp}. A minimum-cardinality certificate exists because the complete finite dataset is a certificate.

We give the positive-basis ingredients directly. For a finite set SS, write pos⁡S\operatorname{pos}S for its nonnegative linear combinations. A positive basis of a vector space is an inclusion-minimal finite set whose positive hull is the whole space.

Lemma 22 (Positive spanning compression and anchors).

In a finite-dimensional real vector space of dimension rr:

  1. 1.

    every nonnegative combination has a representation on a linearly independent subset;

  2. 2.

    a positive basis has at most 2​r2r elements;

  3. 3.

    if SS positively spans the space and C⊆SC\subseteq S positively spans its own aa-dimensional span, then some T⊆ST\subseteq S positively spans the whole space and satisfies |T|≤|C|+2​(r−a)|T|\leq|C|+2(r-a);

  4. 4.

    a positive basis of size 2​r−j2r-j, j≥1j\geq 1, contains a positively balanced simplex of dimension aa with 2≤a≤j+12\leq a\leq j+1.

Proof.

For the first assertion, a dependence among the currently positive coefficients permits a coefficient adjustment along a nonzero zero relation. Orient the relation so that one coefficient is positive, and subtract the smallest ratio of a current coefficient to a positive relation coefficient. Nonnegativity and the represented vector are preserved, and the support strictly decreases. Iteration proves the claim.

Choose a linear basis BB from a positive basis SS. Represent −∑b∈Bb-\sum_{b\in B}b nonnegatively on an independent subset T⊆ST\subseteq S, so |T|≤r|T|\leq r. Every −b-b belongs to pos⁡(B∪T)\operatorname{pos}(B\cup T). Hence B∪TB\cup T positively spans the whole space, and minimality gives S=B∪TS=B\cup T, proving |S|≤2​r|S|\leq 2r.

For the third assertion, let W=span⁡CW=\operatorname{span}C. The image of SS positively spans the quotient by WW. Choose a positive basis there, of size at most 2​(r−a)2(r-a), and one original representative per quotient vector. Their nonnegative combinations represent every quotient class. Subtract such a representative combination from the desired vector; the remainder lies in WW and is a nonnegative combination of CC. The union has the required size and positive span. In particular, if SS itself is a positive basis, minimality implies

|S|≤|C|+2​(r−a).|S|\leq|C|+2(r-a). (C.1)

For each x∈Sx\in S, represent −x-x by a strictly positive combination of an independent subset T⊆ST\subseteq S. Then x∉Tx\notin T, and C=T∪{x}C=T\cup\{x\} is a balanced simplex with dimension |T||T|. A positive basis contains no zero vector, so |T|≥1|T|\geq 1. If every such simplex had dimension one, each generator would have an opposite positive multiple in SS. A linear basis and its opposite partners would positively span the space and would consist of exactly 2​r2r distinct vectors. Minimality would give |S|=2​r|S|=2r, a contradiction. Thus some simplex has a≥2a\geq 2. Applying (C.1) with |S|=2​r−j|S|=2r-j and |C|=a+1|C|=a+1 gives a≤j+1a\leq j+1. ∎

Lemma 23 (Full-rank certificate alternatives).

Suppose U=ℝdU=\mathbb{R}^{d}, d>0d>0. For a budget 2​d−t2d-t, either an exact full-span selection fits the budget, a minimum certificate has 2​d2d active rows, or there is a balanced anchor CC whose feature span has dimension aa, with either (a,|C|)=(1,1)(a,|C|)=(1,1) or 2≤a≤t2\leq a\leq t, |C|=a+1|C|=a+1.

Proof.

Choose a minimum certificate BB. No row in BB has zero feature: removing it would preserve balance and span, and the remaining support is nonempty because the feature rank is positive. If some gi=0g_{i}=0 on BB, its nonzero feature is a singleton balanced anchor of dimension one. Otherwise its gradients and features have the same span. Strict positive balance makes the gradients positively span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. They form a positive basis with distinct vectors: a smaller positively spanning set, or one representative for each repeated gradient, would give a smaller full-span certificate. Lemma 22 gives |B|≤2​d|B|\leq 2d. If 2​d−t<|B|<2​d2d-t<|B|<2d, write |B|=2​d−j|B|=2d-j, 1≤j<t1\leq j<t, and use its simplex anchor. Nonzero collinearity of gradients and features preserves the anchor dimension and its original row count. The other two cardinality cases give the stated alternatives. ∎

C.2 The maximum-cardinality branch uses the complete dataset

The following argument includes gradients outside the chosen certificate. Suppose a minimum full-span certificate has 2​d2d active rows. Their gradients positively span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, so the full gradient set SS does too. Every positively spanning subset of SS has at least 2​d2d elements: choose one original row per vector, use strict positive balance, and observe that spanning gradients imply spanning features.

Consequently every balanced simplex C⊆SC\subseteq S has dimension at most one. Otherwise Lemma 22(3) gives a positively spanning set of size at most (a+1)+2​(d−a)<2​d(a+1)+2(d-a)<2d. Choose a positive basis B⊆SB\subseteq S. For any nonzero x∈Sx\in S, an independent positive representation of −x-x using BB gives a simplex through xx. It must use a single vector, so xx has an opposite positive multiple in BB. In particular every element of BB has a partner. Choose a linear basis from BB and these partners; their union positively spans the space, so minimality makes it all of BB. Every gradient in the complete dataset therefore lies on one of these dd independent lines.

If a nonzero feature anywhere in the dataset has zero gradient, use it as a singleton anchor in the induction below. In the remaining case, every nonzero feature lies on the same independent lines. Write xi=αi​vj⁡(i)x_{i}=\alpha_{i}v_{j(i)}, with v1,…,vdv_{1},\ldots,v_{d} a linear basis, and ri=xi⊤​w⋆−yir_{i}=x_{i}^{\top}w^{\star}-y_{i}. For the nonzero rows on line jj, put

Hj=∑i:j⁡(i)=jpiαi2,Rj=∑i:j⁡(i)=jpiri2.H_{j}=\sum_{i:j(i)=j}p_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2},\qquad R_{j}=\sum_{i:j(i)=j}p_{i}r_{i}^{2}.

The basis coordinates w↦(vj⊤​w)jw\mapsto(v_{j}^{\top}w)_{j} are invertible, even when the lines are not orthogonal. The full normal equation balances each line separately. Two original rows suffice to keep its coordinate unchanged: use one zero-gradient row if present, or balance two oppositely signed scalar gradients with positive weights.

One row can set the displacement coordinate to uj=−ri/αiu_{j}=-r_{i}/\alpha_{i}. Its smallest excess δj\delta_{j} obeys 0≤δj≤Rj0\leq\delta_{j}\leq R_{j}, because the average of Hj​(ri/αi)2H_{j}(r_{i}/\alpha_{i})^{2} under probabilities pi​αi2/Hjp_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2}/H_{j} is exactly RjR_{j}. Compress the tt least costly lines to one row and keep at most two rows on each other line. Their union spans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, their local normal equations combine, and normalizing all weights leaves the minimizer unchanged. Thus

|supp⁡(q)|≤2​d−t,LD​(w^​(q))−LD⋆=∑j​ compressedδj≤td​∑jδj≤td​∑jRj≤td​LD⋆.|\operatorname{supp}(q)|\leq 2d-t,\qquad L_{D}(\widehat{w}(q))-L_{D}^{\star}=\sum_{j\text{ compressed}}\delta_{j}\leq\frac{t}{d}\sum_{j}\delta_{j}\leq\frac{t}{d}\sum_{j}R_{j}\leq\frac{t}{d}L_{D}^{\star}. (C.2)

Zero features contribute only a nonnegative constant to the evaluation loss. Every line retains a nonzero feature, so this construction returns the required minimum-norm fit.

C.3 Balanced anchors and an actual positive-weight limit

Let U=ℝdU=\mathbb{R}^{d} and let normalized weights β\beta on an anchor CC balance the gradients at w⋆w^{\star}. Write W=span⁡{xi:i∈C}W=\operatorname{span}\{x_{i}:i\in C\}, E=W⟂E=W^{\perp}, and let P,QP,Q be the respective orthogonal projections. Suppose a projected selection γ\gamma spans EE and returns z∈Ez\in E. Set A=∑iβi​xi​xi⊤A=\sum_{i}\beta_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}, B=∑iγi​xi​xi⊤B=\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}, and b=∑iγi​ri​xib=\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}r_{i}x_{i}. Then Q⁡(B​z+b)=0Q(Bz+b)=0. For 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, use

qϵ=(1−ϵ)​β+ϵ​γ.q_{\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon)\beta+\epsilon\gamma.

Mϵ=(1−ϵ)​A+ϵ​P​B+Q​B,fϵ=−(ϵ​P+Q)​b.M_{\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon)A+\epsilon PB+QB,\qquad f_{\epsilon}=-(\epsilon P+Q)b. (C.3)

Since A​z=0Az=0 and Q⁡(B​z+b)=0Q(Bz+b)=0, we have M0​z=f0M_{0}z=f_{0}. Continuity of matrix inversion gives uϵ=Mϵ−1​fϵ→zu_{\epsilon}=M_{\epsilon}^{-1}f_{\epsilon}\to z. Moreover,

LD​(w⋆+z)=∑ipi​(ri+xi⊤​z)2=L¯​(z).L_{D}(w^{\star}+z)=\sum_{i}p_{i}(r_{i}+x_{i}^{\top}z)^{2}=\bar{L}(z).
